Research task (web), no code changes. I'm designing an interaction-motion identity for Twyne, a literary writing app (local-first rich-text editor + an AI "room of editors" that leave margin notes, a rubric that "stamps" a draft, a stats "Desk" page). Brand: editorial letterpress — paper, ink, type, stamps, vermilion and cobalt, a writers' room. I want motion, shaders and component variants that (a) communicate what an interaction does and whether you should/shouldn't do it (consequence: local vs synced vs sent to an AI provider vs published vs destructive), (b) make the app feel alive, (c) never harm writing performance or legibility, (d) are distinctive versus generic editors (Notion, Google Docs, Word).

Please find and summarise, with source URLs:
1. "Game feel"/"juice" principles applied to productivity UI (e.g. Jonasson & Purho "Juice it or lose it", Rauno Freiberg "Invisible details of interaction design", Emil Kowalski on animation craft, Linear/Raycast/Arc/Things motion writing, Apple HIG motion). Extract concrete, reusable rules (durations, easing, when not to animate, frequency of interaction vs animation budget).
2. Editors with distinctive typing/caret/scroll feel: Microsoft Word smooth caret/typing animation, VS Code smooth caret, iA Writer focus/typewriter mode, Ulysses, Bear, Craft, Obsidian, Monkeytype caret, Typora, Hemingway, Paper by WeTransfer/FiftyThree, Teenage Engineering-style UIs. What exactly do they animate and how is it received (any complaints about distraction/latency)?
3. Ink, paper and letterpress effects on the web: ink-bleed / wet-ink shaders, paper grain/fibre normal maps lit by a moving light, letterpress debossing via CSS, risograph/halftone shaders, stamp impressions. Prefer techniques that are cheap (WebGL fragment shaders at reduced resolution, CSS only, SVG filters) and note performance pitfalls (SVG filters on large areas, backdrop-filter).
4. Modern browser APIs useful here, with current support status (2025-2026): CSS Custom Highlight API (`::highlight()` — which properties are allowed, can it animate?), View Transitions API (same-document), scroll-driven animations (`animation-timeline: scroll()/view()`), `@property` registered custom properties for animating gradients, `linear()` easing for springs, Popover API + `@starting-style`, `interpolate-size`, WebGPU vs WebGL2 availability.
5. Patterns that communicate consequence/trust in UI motion: hold-to-confirm for destructive actions, "sending" vs "saving" animations, rate-limit/out-of-credits states, disabled-with-reason affordances, AI "thinking" indicators that aren't generic spinners (e.g. shimmer text, reading-progress indicators). Note which are considered good vs gimmicky.
6. Anything about "ambient life" in UI: presence indicators (Figma cursors), breathing idle states, time-of-day lighting, and accessibility guidance (prefers-reduced-motion, vestibular triggers, WCAG 2.3.3, avoiding parallax for long reading).

Deliver a compact report (under ~1500 words): bullet points grouped by the six headings, each bullet with a concrete takeaway and a URL. Flag anything you could not verify. Finish with a list of 10 "gaps": ideas that fit a literary editor + AI editors and are rarely done well elsewhere.

tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).
- Subagents run in the background by default; you'll be notified when one completes. Pass `run_in_background: false` only when your very next action depends on the result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — otherwise background it so the user can interject. tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).
- Subagents run in the background by default; you'll be notified when one completes. Pass `run_in_background: false` only when your very next action depends on the result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — otherwise background it so the user can interject. Never fabricate or predict a pending agent's results — the notification is never something you write yourself; if the user asks before it arrives, say it's still running.

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.
